seoDescription: Explore the concept of signals for state management and UI updates in modern web development. Learn how signals, a pattern popularized by frameworks like Vue.js (as refs), SolidJS, Angular, and Svelte (with runes), enable fine-grained reactivity for improved performance. This video breaks down how signals work internally, explaining the core principles of subscribers and effects, and guides you through building a basic signal from scratch to understand how data changes trigger specific UI updates.

summary:
## What Are Signals?

- **Signals** are a pattern for state management and UI updates that has become prevalent in modern web frameworks.
- They were introduced in **Vue 3** (as `refs`), popularized by **SolidJS**, and subsequently adopted by frameworks like **Angular** and **Svelte** (with `runes`).
- A signal wraps a piece of state and ensures that any part of the UI using that state is automatically updated when the value changes.

## The Core Benefit: Fine-Grained Reactivity

- The main advantage of signals is enabling **fine-grained reactivity**.
- This means that when a signal's value changes, only the specific parts of the UI that depend on it are updated, rather than re-rendering an entire component tree.
- This targeted update mechanism leads to greater **efficiency** and **better performance**.

## How Signals Work: A Basic Implementation

A signal system can be understood by breaking it down into three core components: a creator function, subscribers, and an effect mechanism.

### 1. The `createSignal` Function

The foundation is a `createSignal` function that accepts an initial value.
- It internally manages the state.
- It returns a pair of functions:
  - A **getter** (or `read`) function to access the current value.
  - A **setter** (or `set`) function to update the value.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> A signal must return a *function* to get the value, not the value itself. The act of calling this function is what allows the signal to identify and register what part of the code is interested in its value.

### 2. Implementing Reactivity with Subscribers

To make signals reactive, we introduce a list of **subscribers**.
- **Subscription**: When a signal's `read` function is called, the entity that called it is added to the signal's internal list of subscribers.
- **Notification**: When the `set` function is called with a new value, it iterates through its list of subscribers and executes each one, notifying them of the change.

### 3. Automatic Subscription with an `effect` Function

Manually managing subscriptions is tedious. The standard solution is a separate `effect` function that automates the process.
- The `effect(fn)` function wraps any code (`fn`) that reads a signal.
- This pattern typically relies on a global variable (e.g., `currentEffect`).
  1. The `effect` function sets the global variable to reference its own execution context (`fn`).
  2. It then runs `fn()`.
  3. Inside `fn`, when a signal's `read` function is called, it checks the global variable and adds the `currentEffect` to its subscriber list.
  4. After `fn` completes, the `effect` function clears the global variable.

> [!TIP]
> This `effect` mechanism is how a signal automatically knows who is listening without you needing to pass callbacks around manually. It creates a seamless link between reading a value and subscribing to its future changes.

## Framework Abstractions

- Real-world frameworks like **Vue**, **Angular**, and **SolidJS** use these same fundamental principles.
- Their implementations are more optimized and feature-rich.
- A key feature is that they often handle the `effect` wrapping for you automatically when you use a signal within a component's template, simplifying the developer experience.
transcription:
## The Rise of Signals in Modern Frameworks

So the idea of using signals for state management and UI updating was already introduced by Vue when Vue.js version 3 was released in 2020. Now the signals pattern was of course not necessarily pioneered by Vue but they were the first major framework to actively use signals for UI updates. Though in Vue signals were called refs.

Still the idea was the same, you could set up a ref, then refer to it in your template and whenever you then change such a ref value that place in the UI where the signal is used will automatically get updated. That's the idea behind signals.

And signals then became really popular even though Vue was using them right from the start when SolidJS embraced them. Even though SolidJS is actually a smaller frontend JavaScript framework but nonetheless it made signals really popular. Maybe because they weren't called signals in Vue or they didn't market them aggressively enough. Whatever. So SolidJS made the concept of fine-grained reactivity where only the parts of the UI that really changed are updated when data changes. Super popular and suddenly everyone wanted to use signals.

## Adoption Across the Ecosystem

For example Angular also introduced signals. Now you can still use Angular the way you always did and signals at the point of time where I'm recording this aren't even fully implemented yet. There still are some features missing which they want to add but still Angular now also has signals and you can use signals to manage your state and get Angular to update your UI.

Svelte for example also introduced runes which are their signals for UI update management. So signals clearly are everywhere.

## Why Signals? The Promise of Fine-Grained Reactivity

And why is that? Well that's the case because of this fine-grained reactivity they allow those frameworks to offer with such a signal-based approach. And that of course can lead to a higher efficiency and better performance.

## Building a Basic Signal: Getters and Setters

But how do signals actually work? That's what I want to take a look at here now and for that we're simply going to build our own basic signal.

Now in a nutshell a signal is simply some data and some function that may update that data combined with a list of subscribers who are interested in data changes so that those subscribers can be notified whenever the data changes.

Therefore if we want to build our own very basic signal library that of course does not have the same amount of features Vue or Angular have, we can start by creating a function that manages some data and that then creates two internal functions. So functions inside of the function. One function that will simply return the latest data and one function that can be used to set that data to a new value.

Now you might wonder why we need a function for getting that signal value and why we don't just return that value and I'll get back to that in a second. And then from our createSignal function we return those two functions. The function for reading the signal and the function for setting the signal value.

In addition in that createSignal function we also accept an initial value so that we can set this internally managed data to an initial value. And then we can use the createSignal function to create multiple signals with their own data. And we can use the read function to read those values and the set function to update those values and then we can read the updated values.

## Introducing Subscribers for Reactivity

So that works but at this point we don't really have any reactivity yet. When we set the signal to a new value the places where we're using it are not notified.

And that's what we can therefore change by also managing a list of subscribers which could be a simple array or a set whatever. Now with that subscribers array set up we can go to that read function and then in there actually push a new subscriber onto that subscribers array. And that's why this read function must be a function and why we don't directly return the signal value in the createSignal function. Because we need to know who's reading and we need to add that thing that place in our code to the subscribers. Though at the moment we're not adding any value yet and I'll get back to this in a second. Let's assume though we would add something here.

In that case we of course would want to notify all subscribers whenever the signal value changes. And that's therefore what we do in that set function. There we simply iterate through all subscribers and then we assume that every subscriber is a function we can call to let that subscriber know that the signal value changed and that it should again do whatever it wants to do with that signal. So our assumption is that a subscriber is a function in the end and we need to add that subscriber function when we read a signal.

## The `effect` Function and Automatic Subscription

Now how do we do that? Well we could accept it as an argument in the read function and that would be a valid way of implementing it. But that way every time we read the signal we would have to pass a function to that read function which is then that subscriber function that will be called when the signal is updated. But that's not necessarily the best way of implementing it.

Instead what's typically done is that you create a separate effect function which then can be used to wrap any code that reads a signal so that you can again read without passing a function to your read function. Because the idea now simply is that this effect function takes a function that should be re-executed every time the read signal changes and that's achieved by inside of that effect function updating some global variable and setting that global variable equal to the effect function then calling read and in the read function we then reach out to that global variable to get the currently executing effect function and we add that currently executing effect function which is stored in that global variable to that subscribers array.

By doing it like this we can then use this effect function how often we want in our code to register a function that will re-execute whenever the signal that's being read inside of it is changing.

Now that read function here will be executed and will add this effect to its subscribers because it's that read function that's executed in the effect function and we make sure that this effect function gets executed after updating this global variable. Therefore the effect function executes in there the read function executes and that read function reaches out to that global variable which refers to that effect function that's currently being executed and adds it to the list of subscribers and that's how we can make sure that all these effect functions we're executing are getting added to the list of subscribers and that is how we could implement our own basic signals library.

## How Frameworks Simplify Signal Usage

Now of course as mentioned those frameworks are of course a bit more advanced and do this in a bit of a more efficient way and also offer extra features. They for example also allow you to use a signal in a template and they automatically wrap it by such a effect function for you. But in a nutshell if you wanted to build your own very basic signal library that's how you could do and that is how signals in the end work under the hood.
